readings.title: Oz, chapter IV, part 1: no place like home
readings.challenge: Weigh one character’s reason against another’s, and notice when a joke also makes a point.
readings.focus: Dorothy explains why people choose a gray home, and the Scarecrow remembers being painted one part at a time.
readings.context: Recap: a cyclone carried Dorothy and Toto to the Land of Oz. They are following the road of yellow brick to the Emerald City, where the Wizard Oz may send her home to Kansas. Dorothy has just lifted the Scarecrow down from his pole in a cornfield, and he has come along to ask Oz for brains. Dreary means gloomy and dull.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “The Road Through the Forest,” from the start through the farmer leaving the Scarecrow in the cornfield; opens “After a few hours the road began to be rough, and the walking grew so difficult that the…”; closes “…stick, where you found me. He and his friend soon after walked away and left me alone.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the Scarecrow keep falling on the broken road when Toto and Dorothy do not?
facilitatorNotes: Toto jumps across the holes and Dorothy walks around them; the Scarecrow, “having no brains,” walks straight ahead. Notice that falling never hurts him and that he laughs at his own mishap.
evidence: having no brains he walked straight ahead
joined her in laughing merrily at his own mishap

questions.prompt: Why does the Scarecrow refuse Dorothy’s bread?
facilitatorNotes: His mouth is only painted. If he cut a hole to eat, the straw would come out and spoil the shape of his head. The reason is funny and also quite sensible.
evidence: For my mouth is only painted

questions.prompt: Dorothy says, “There is no place like home.” What reason does she give, and what does the Scarecrow decide from it?
facilitatorNotes: She says people of flesh and blood would rather live at home, however gray. The Scarecrow says straw-headed people would all live in beautiful places, so it is lucky for Kansas that people have brains. Some children will side with Dorothy; others may enjoy his joke that brains make people choose the dull place.
evidence: No matter how dreary and gray our homes are
It is fortunate for Kansas that you have brains.

questions.prompt: The farmer paints the Scarecrow one part at a time. What can the Scarecrow do after each part is painted?
facilitatorNotes: Ears first, so he hears the farmer; then one eye, and he looks around with curiosity; a bigger second eye, so he sees better; then a mouth, though he does not speak because he does not know what a mouth is for. He meets the world one sense at a time.
evidence: one of the first things he did was to paint my ears, so that I heard what was going on
I didn't know what a mouth was for

readings.title: Oz, chapter IV, part 2: the old crow’s advice
readings.challenge: Follow a story told inside the story, and test what a character says about himself against what he does.
readings.focus: An old crow persuades the Scarecrow that brains are worth having; then the travellers enter a dark forest.
readings.context: Recap: walking the yellow brick road, the Scarecrow has begun telling Dorothy his life story. The farmer painted his ears, eyes and mouth, set him on a pole in the cornfield and walked away. Untilled land has not been ploughed or planted.

excerpt.locator: Chapter IV, “The Road Through the Forest,” from the crows in the cornfield to the end of the chapter; opens “"I did not like to be deserted this way; so I tried to walk after them, but my feet would…”; closes “…who was never tired, stood up in another corner and waited patiently until morning came.”.

questions.prompt: How do the crows find out that the Scarecrow is not a real man?
facilitatorNotes: An old crow looks at him carefully, perches on his shoulder and eats the corn. When the other birds see he is not harmed, they come too. The crow tested the scarecrow instead of simply flying away.
evidence: after looking at me carefully he perched upon my shoulder
seeing he was not harmed by me

questions.prompt: The crow says brains are “the only things worth having in this world.” What does the Scarecrow decide to do about it?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks it over and decides to try hard to get some brains, which is why he is going to Oz. Children may notice that this advice comes from the crow who has just eaten his corn, and wonder whether the crow is a good adviser.
evidence: Brains are the only things worth having in this world
decided I would try hard to get some brains

questions.prompt: The Scarecrow says, “If this road goes in, it must come out.” Is that a brainless thing to say?
facilitatorNotes: It is good reasoning. When Dorothy says anyone would know it, he answers that this is exactly why he knows it. He keeps thinking well and then saying he cannot think.
evidence: If this road goes in, it must come out
If it required brains to figure it out, I never should have said it.

questions.prompt: In the dark forest, who can see and who cannot? How does the group manage?
facilitatorNotes: Dorothy cannot see; Toto and the Scarecrow can. She holds his arm, and he finds the cottage. The friend who says he knows nothing is the one who leads.
evidence: Dorothy could not see at all, but Toto could
So she took hold of his arm, and managed to get along fairly well.

readings.title: Oz, chapter V, part 1: a groan in the forest
readings.challenge: Follow a rescue step by step and notice what each helper does.
readings.focus: Dorothy and the Scarecrow free a rusted tin man, one joint at a time.
readings.context: Recap: a cyclone carried Dorothy and her dog Toto to the Land of Oz, and they are following the yellow brick road to ask the Wizard Oz to send her home to Kansas. The Scarecrow has joined them to ask for brains. They spent the night in an empty cottage in a dark forest. Rust is the reddish crust that forms on iron when it gets wet and makes it stiff.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “The Rescue of the Tin Woodman,” from the start through oiling the Tin Woodman’s legs; opens “When Dorothy awoke the sun was shining through the trees and Toto had long been out…”; closes “…again and again for his release, for he seemed a very polite creature, and very grateful.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the Scarecrow think it must be “inconvenient to be made of flesh”?
facilitatorNotes: People must sleep, eat and drink. He adds that brains are worth all that bother. Ask whether he would trade his straw for flesh.
evidence: for you must sleep, and eat and drink

questions.prompt: What tells Dorothy that someone nearby needs help, even before she sees him?
facilitatorNotes: First a deep groan, then another groan behind them, then something shining in a ray of sunshine. Sound comes first and sight second.
evidence: she was startled to hear a deep groan near by
something shining in a ray of sunshine

questions.prompt: How long has the tin man been standing still, and what is the first thing he is glad to do?
facilitatorNotes: More than a year, groaning with no one to hear. Once his arms move, he puts down the axe he has held in the air all that time. Children can imagine holding an arm up for a year.
evidence: I've been groaning for more than a year, and no one has ever heard me before
I have been holding that axe in the air ever since I rusted

questions.prompt: Dorothy does the oiling, but the Scarecrow does something too. Why does the rescue need both of them?
facilitatorNotes: Oil alone does not free the joints; the Scarecrow moves the head from side to side and bends the arms until they work. Their two jobs fit together.
evidence: the Scarecrow took hold of the tin head and moved it gently from side to side
the Scarecrow bent them carefully

readings.title: Oz, chapter V, part 2: a third traveller
readings.challenge: Notice how a new character’s wish echoes the others’, and what he adds to the company.
readings.focus: The Tin Woodman joins the party, clears the road, and says a heart is better than brains.
readings.context: Recap: in the forest Dorothy and the Scarecrow found a man made of tin, rusted so stiff he could not move, and oiled his joints until he could. A comrade is a companion.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “The Rescue of the Tin Woodman,” from the Tin Woodman’s thanks to the start of his story; opens “"I might have stood there always if you had not come along," he said; "so you have…”; closes “"I will tell you my story, and then you will know."”.

questions.prompt: What does the Tin Woodman ask after he hears why the others are going to Oz?
facilitatorNotes: Whether Oz could give him a heart. Dorothy guesses it would be as easy as giving the Scarecrow brains; she does not yet know how hard any of these wishes will be.
evidence: Do you suppose Oz could give me a heart?
it would be as easy as to give the Scarecrow brains

questions.prompt: Why does the Tin Woodman ask Dorothy to carry the oil-can?
facilitatorNotes: Rain could rust him again. He is planning for a danger he already knows. Children may guess that the oil-can will be needed later.
evidence: if I should get caught in the rain, and rust again, I would need the oil-can badly

questions.prompt: How does the Tin Woodman prove useful almost at once?
facilitatorNotes: Branches grow so thick over the road that no one can pass, and his axe clears a way. The narrator calls it good luck to have him.
evidence: chopped so well that soon he cleared a passage for the entire party

questions.prompt: The Scarecrow wants brains and the Tin Woodman would rather have a heart. Why might the Tin Woodman’s opinion count for more?
facilitatorNotes: He says he once had both, so he has “tried them both”; the Scarecrow has never had either. Some children will say trying both makes him the better judge; others may say his opinion is still only his own.
evidence: once I had brains, and a heart also; so, having tried them both, I should much rather have a heart.

readings.title: Oz, chapter V, part 3: the Tin Woodman’s story
readings.challenge: Follow a long story told by one character, then weigh two friends’ opposite answers.
readings.focus: A witch takes the woodman’s body piece by piece, and the loss he minds most is his heart.
readings.context: Recap: the Tin Woodman, freed from rust, has joined Dorothy and the Scarecrow on the road to Oz. He told the Scarecrow he once had brains and a heart and would rather have a heart, and now he explains why. Munchkins are the little people of the eastern part of Oz; a tinsmith or tinner makes things of tin.
readings.contentNote: In his story an enchanted axe cuts off the woodman’s legs, arms and head one at a time and splits his body; the telling is fanciful and bloodless.

excerpt.locator: Chapter V, “The Rescue of the Tin Woodman,” the Tin Woodman’s story to the end of the chapter; opens “So, while they were walking through the forest, the Tin Woodman told the following story:”; closes “…anything, but she was not made of tin nor straw, and could not live unless she was fed.”.

questions.prompt: Why did the old woman want to stop the marriage, and what did she pay the Witch?
facilitatorNotes: She was so lazy she wanted the girl to stay and do the cooking and housework, and she promised two sheep and a cow. Selfishness, not danger, starts the trouble.
evidence: she was so lazy she wished the girl to remain with her
promised her two sheep and a cow

questions.prompt: Each time the axe slips, what does the woodman do next? What does that show about him?
facilitatorNotes: He goes back to the tinsmith for a new tin part and keeps chopping, “nothing daunted,” because he wants to build the house and marry. Some children call that brave; others call it stubborn.
evidence: nothing daunted, I had them replaced with tin ones
I thought I had beaten the wicked Witch then

questions.prompt: Of everything he lost, which loss does the Tin Woodman call the greatest, and why?
facilitatorNotes: His heart, because without one he cannot love. He worked this out while he stood rusted for a year. His shining tin body made him proud, yet the loss he minds is one no one can see.
evidence: the greatest loss I had known was the loss of my heart
no one can love who has not a heart

questions.prompt: Who do you think is right, the Scarecrow or the Tin Woodman? What does Dorothy think?
facilitatorNotes: The Scarecrow says a fool would not know what to do with a heart; the Woodman says brains do not make anyone happy. Dorothy is puzzled and mostly worried about the bread running out. Both friends can be defended, and her practical worry is a third answer.
evidence: a fool would not know what to do with a heart if he had one
brains do not make one happy, and happiness is the best thing in the world
she was puzzled to know which of her two friends was right

readings.title: Oz, chapter VI, part 1: a roar in the forest
readings.challenge: Notice when a character’s actions and words do not agree.
readings.focus: A great Lion attacks, Dorothy slaps his nose, and he admits he is a coward.
readings.context: Recap: Dorothy and her dog Toto are walking the yellow brick road through a forest to the Emerald City, to ask the Wizard Oz to send her home to Kansas. With her are the Scarecrow, who wants brains, and the Tin Woodman, who wants a heart. Earlier, the good Witch of the North kissed Dorothy’s forehead and said the mark would protect her. People have long called the lion the King of Beasts.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “The Cowardly Lion,” from the start through the Lion explaining how roaring has kept him safe; opens “All this time Dorothy and her companions had been walking through the thick woods. The…”; closes “…soon as they hear me roar they all try to get away from me, and of course I let them go."”.

questions.prompt: Who does the Tin Woodman say is safe in the forest, and who is not? What does he say they must do?
facilitatorNotes: He has his oil-can, nothing can hurt the Scarecrow, and Dorothy has the good Witch’s kiss; Toto has nothing, so they must protect him themselves. Listen for how this sets up what happens next.
evidence: We must protect him ourselves, if he is in danger

questions.prompt: The Lion is as big as a small horse. Why does Dorothy slap him?
facilitatorNotes: She is afraid Toto will be killed and rushes forward “heedless of danger.” She acts from love for Toto, not because she knows she is safe. Some children call it brave; others call it rash.
evidence: fearing Toto would be killed, and heedless of danger

questions.prompt: Why does Dorothy call Toto “a meat dog”?
facilitatorNotes: The Lion asks whether Toto is tin or stuffed, so she has to find words for an ordinary dog made of flesh. The joke is that in this company, being made of meat is the unusual thing.
evidence: Is he made of tin, or stuffed?
He's a—a—a meat dog

questions.prompt: How has the Lion managed to seem brave all his life?
facilitatorNotes: He roars, and every creature runs away, so he never has to fight. His fame comes from noise, not courage. Ask whether the animals who run are braver than he is.
evidence: I learned that if I roared very loudly every living thing was frightened and got out of my way

readings.title: Oz, chapter VI, part 2: a beetle on the road
readings.challenge: Hear a pattern of repeated lines, and decide what a careful action shows about a character.
readings.focus: The Lion joins the journey to ask for courage, and the Tin Woodman, who says he has no heart, weeps over a beetle.
readings.context: Recap: in the forest a great Lion attacked the travellers until Dorothy slapped his nose for trying to bite Toto. Then he admitted that he is a coward and has only seemed brave by roaring.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VI, “The Cowardly Lion,” from the Scarecrow’s answer to the end of the chapter; opens “"But that isn't right. The King of Beasts shouldn't be a coward," said the Scarecrow.”; closes “…so I must be very careful. When Oz gives me a heart of course I needn't mind so much."”.

questions.prompt: Why does the Tin Woodman say the Lion ought to be glad if he has heart disease?
facilitatorNotes: It would prove the Lion has a heart, the thing the Woodman wants most. He looks at the Lion’s trouble through his own wish.
evidence: for it proves you have a heart

questions.prompt: Listen to the four friends answer one another about Oz. What pattern do you hear?
facilitatorNotes: Each says a wish in turn: brains, a heart, Kansas, and then courage, with “Just as easily,” “Or give me,” “Or send me.” The repeated lines make four travellers into one company with a shared hope.
evidence: Just as easily as he could give me brains
Or give me a heart
Or send me back to Kansas

questions.prompt: What happens after the Tin Woodman steps on a beetle, and what does he do differently afterwards?
facilitatorNotes: He weeps, his tears rust his jaws shut, and the Scarecrow oils them. From then on he watches the road and steps over even a tiny ant.
evidence: crying rusts my jaw so that I cannot speak
when he saw a tiny ant toiling by he would step over it

questions.prompt: The Tin Woodman says he has no heart, yet he cries over a beetle. Does he have a heart or not?
facilitatorNotes: He explains that he must be extra careful because he has no heart to guide him. Many children will say his kindness shows the very heart he thinks he lacks; others will take his explanation at its word. Either way, the reader notices something he does not.
evidence: he took great care never to be cruel or unkind to anything
You people with hearts

readings.title: Oz, chapter VII, part 1: a leap across the ditch
readings.challenge: Follow a problem and its solution, and notice who thinks of what.
readings.focus: Each traveller gives what he can: nuts from the Scarecrow, a fire from the Woodman’s wood, a great leap from the Lion.
readings.context: Recap: Dorothy, her dog Toto, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion are walking to the Emerald City to ask the great Wizard Oz for help: Dorothy wants to go home to Kansas, the Scarecrow wants brains, the Tin Woodman a heart and the Lion courage. They are still in a thick forest on the yellow brick road. A gulf here is a deep ditch.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “The Journey to The Great Oz,” from the night under the tree through the Lion’s three leaps; opens “They were obliged to camp out that night under a large tree in the forest, for there were…”; closes “…had made his breath short, and he panted like a big dog that has been running too long.”.

questions.prompt: Dorothy’s bread is gone. What do the Lion and the Scarecrow each offer her, and which offer upsets the Tin Woodman?
facilitatorNotes: The Lion offers to kill a deer for her breakfast; the Woodman begs him not to, because he would weep and rust. The Scarecrow fills her basket with nuts.
evidence: Don't! please don't
found a tree full of nuts and filled Dorothy's basket

questions.prompt: Why doesn’t the Scarecrow mind how long it takes him to pick up the nuts?
facilitatorNotes: The slow job keeps him away from the fire, which could set his straw alight. A clumsy job is also a safe one.
evidence: it enabled him to keep away from the fire

questions.prompt: Why does the Scarecrow say he should be the first to cross on the Lion’s back?
facilitatorNotes: If the Lion fell short, Dorothy would be killed or the Woodman dented, but a fall could not hurt the Scarecrow. That is careful thinking from someone who says he has no brains.
evidence: But if I am on your back it will not matter so much, for the fall would not hurt me at all.

questions.prompt: The Lion says he is terribly afraid of falling. What does he do anyway, and what might that say about courage?
facilitatorNotes: He jumps the ditch again and again until everyone is across. He is afraid and does it anyway. Children can say whether that is courage, or wait to see what the book decides.
evidence: I am terribly afraid of falling, myself
there is nothing to do but try it

readings.title: Oz, chapter VII, part 2: the Kalidahs
readings.challenge: Track a quick run of dangers and find the idea that saves the party.
readings.focus: A fallen tree becomes a bridge and then a trap, and the frightened Lion stands and roars.
readings.context: Recap: the Lion carried his friends one at a time across a deep ditch in the forest, though he was afraid of falling. Now they hear strange noises ahead.
readings.contentNote: Two fierce beasts chase the travellers and are killed when they fall with a tree onto the rocks of a ditch.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VII, “The Journey to The Great Oz,” from the dark forest beyond the ditch to the end of the chapter; opens “They found the forest very thick on this side, and it looked dark and gloomy. After the…”; closes “…City, and of the good Wizard Oz, who would soon send her back to her own home again.”.

questions.prompt: What are the Kalidahs, as the Lion describes them?
facilitatorNotes: Beasts with bodies like bears, heads like tigers and long sharp claws. Hearing the Lion’s fear first makes them sound worse before they appear.
evidence: They are monstrous beasts with bodies like bears and heads like tigers

questions.prompt: The Scarecrow has two ideas about the same tree. What are they?
facilitatorNotes: First, chop it down so it falls across the ditch as a bridge; later, chop off its end so it drops into the gulf with the Kalidahs on it. The Lion’s joke that he “almost” has brains comes true twice.
evidence: If the Tin Woodman can chop it down
One would almost suspect you had brains in your head

questions.prompt: The Lion begins to tremble when he sees the Kalidahs. What does he do next?
facilitatorNotes: He turns to face them, roars so loudly that they stop, and promises to fight as long as he is alive. He is frightened and brave at the same moment.
evidence: stand close behind me, and I will fight them as long as I am alive

questions.prompt: After the danger, the Lion says his heart is still beating, and the Tin Woodman answers sadly. Why does that small exchange matter?
facilitatorNotes: The Woodman wishes he had a heart to beat, even a frightened one. Each friend hears the same event through his own wish.
evidence: my heart is beating yet
I wish I had a heart to beat

readings.title: Oz, chapter VIII, part 1: swept down the river
readings.challenge: Follow a plan that goes wrong, and listen for a pattern that returns from earlier in the book.
readings.focus: The river carries the raft off course and leaves the Scarecrow stuck on a pole in the middle of the water.
readings.context: Recap: Dorothy, her dog Toto, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion are walking to the Emerald City to ask the great Wizard Oz for help: Dorothy wants to go home to Kansas, the Scarecrow wants brains, the Tin Woodman a heart and the Lion courage. After escaping the fierce Kalidahs in the forest, they reached a broad river, and the Tin Woodman built a raft. A current is the strong flow of water in a river.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, “The Deadly Poppy Field,” from the start through the walk back along the bank; opens “Our little party of travellers awakened next morning refreshed and full of hope, and…”; closes “…and had they not felt so sorry for the poor Scarecrow they could have been very happy.”.

questions.prompt: Listen to the four sentences that begin with “And I should.” What is each traveller afraid of losing?
facilitatorNotes: Brains, courage, a heart and the way back to Kansas: the same four wishes the friends repeated when the Lion joined them, now spoken as fears.
evidence: And then I should get no brains
And I should never get back to Kansas

questions.prompt: How does the Scarecrow end up alone in the middle of the river?
facilitatorNotes: He pushes so hard on his pole that it sticks in the mud, and the raft is swept away while he hangs on. Trying hardest to help is what strands him.
evidence: he pushed so hard on his long pole that it stuck fast in the mud

questions.prompt: The Scarecrow thinks he is now worse off than when he was in the cornfield. Why?
facilitatorNotes: In the cornfield he could at least pretend to scare crows; on a pole in a river he is of no use at all. He judges himself by being useful.
evidence: there is no use for a Scarecrow stuck on a pole in the middle of a river

questions.prompt: How do the others get to shore, and why can’t they enjoy the lovely country afterwards?
facilitatorNotes: The Lion swims with the Tin Woodman holding his tail, and Dorothy pushes with a pole. They are too sorry about the Scarecrow to be happy.
evidence: hold fast to the tip of my tail
had they not felt so sorry for the poor Scarecrow they could have been very happy

readings.title: Oz, chapter VIII, part 2: the kind Stork
readings.challenge: Notice how a weakness from earlier turns into a help.
readings.focus: A passing Stork carries the Scarecrow back to his friends.
readings.context: Recap: the river swept the raft downstream and left the Scarecrow clinging to a pole in the middle of the water. The others reached the shore far below and are walking back up the bank.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, “The Deadly Poppy Field,” from seeing the Scarecrow on his pole through the Stork flying away; opens “They walked along as fast as they could, Dorothy only stopping once to pick a beautiful…”; closes “…replied Dorothy, and then the kind Stork flew into the air and was soon out of sight.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the Stork worry about carrying the Scarecrow, and why does Dorothy say she need not?
facilitatorNotes: The Stork fears he is too heavy and says she might have to drop him. Dorothy explains that he is stuffed with straw. The lightness that made him tumble so easily now saves him.
evidence: If he wasn't so big and heavy I would get him for you
He isn't heavy a bit

questions.prompt: How does the Scarecrow show how glad he is to be back?
facilitatorNotes: He hugs everyone, even the Lion and Toto, and sings “Tol-de-ri-de-oh!” at every step.
evidence: he hugged them all, even the Lion and Toto

questions.prompt: What does the Scarecrow promise the Stork, and how does she answer?
facilitatorNotes: He promises to do her a kindness in return if he ever gets brains. She says she always likes to help anyone in trouble. Ask whether a person needs brains to repay a kindness, and whether the Stork wants to be repaid at all.
evidence: if I ever get any brains I shall find the Stork again and do it some kindness in return
I always like to help anyone in trouble

readings.title: Oz, chapter VIII, part 3: the deadly poppy field
readings.challenge: Notice when the narrator tells readers something a character does not know.
readings.focus: A beautiful field of poppies puts Dorothy, Toto and the Lion to sleep, and their friends must decide what they can do.
readings.context: Recap: a kind Stork lifted the Scarecrow off his pole in the river and carried him back to his friends. Now they are walking through flowery country to find the yellow brick road again. Scarlet is bright red; an odor is a smell.
readings.contentNote: The poppies’ scent puts Dorothy, Toto and the Lion into a sleep that could kill them; the chapter ends with the Lion left behind asleep.

excerpt.locator: Chapter VIII, “The Deadly Poppy Field,” from the meadow of flowers to the end of the chapter; opens “They walked along listening to the singing of the bright-colored birds and looking at the…”; closes “…here they laid her gently on the soft grass and waited for the fresh breeze to waken her.”.

questions.prompt: What does each of Dorothy’s three friends say about the flowers? How do their answers fit their wishes?
facilitatorNotes: The Scarecrow will like them better when he has brains, the Tin Woodman would love them if he had a heart, and the Lion has always liked flowers because they seem “helpless and frail.” Each answer comes from the speaker’s own wish or nature.
evidence: When I have brains I shall probably like them better
If I only had a heart I should love them
they seem so helpless and frail

questions.prompt: The narrator tells us something about poppies that Dorothy does not know. What is it, and how does it change the way the lovely field feels?
facilitatorNotes: Their smell makes sleepers sleep on forever. Because the reader knows the danger before Dorothy does, the beautiful field becomes frightening.
evidence: But Dorothy did not know this

questions.prompt: Why can the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman carry Dorothy out when the Lion cannot stay awake?
facilitatorNotes: They are not made of flesh, so the scent cannot touch them. The straw and tin bodies they wish to change are exactly what save Dorothy.
evidence: not being made of flesh, were not troubled by the scent of the flowers

questions.prompt: Leaving the Lion asleep among the poppies is a hard choice. Do you think it was the right one?
facilitatorNotes: He is far too heavy to lift, and the plan to run ahead was a fair one. Some children will want the friends to try anyway; others will say they must save Dorothy first. The next chapter answers what happens.
evidence: We can do nothing for him
for he is much too heavy to lift

readings.title: Oz, chapter X, part 1: the green country
readings.challenge: Notice how a place changes as travellers get closer to where they are going.
readings.focus: The Lion wakes from the poppies, and the friends reach a land where everything is green.
readings.context: Dorothy, her dog Toto, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion are walking to the Emerald City to ask the great Wizard Oz for help: Dorothy wants to go home to Kansas, the Scarecrow wants brains, the Tin Woodman a heart and the Lion courage. In the last chapter the Queen of the Field Mice and her mice pulled the sleeping Lion out of the poppy field on a little truck. Comrades are friends; fragrance is a smell; to rejoice is to be glad.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, “The Guardian of the Gates,” from the Lion’s waking to the farm woman’s welcome; opens “It was some time before the Cowardly Lion awakened, for he had lain among the poppies a…”; closes “…that is the case you may come in, and I will give you some supper and a place to sleep."”.

questions.prompt: What does the Lion find strange about how he was nearly killed and how he was saved?
facilitatorNotes: Small things, flowers, nearly killed him, and small animals, mice, saved him, though he always thought himself big and terrible.
evidence: such small things as flowers came near to killing me, and such small animals as mice have saved my life

questions.prompt: What clues tell Dorothy they are nearly at the Emerald City?
facilitatorNotes: The fences, the farmhouses and the people’s clothes are all green, just as blue was the color in the Munchkin country.
evidence: everything is green here, while in the country of the Munchkins blue was the favorite color

questions.prompt: Why do the people stay away from the travellers?
facilitatorNotes: They are afraid of the great Lion.
evidence: no one came near them nor spoke to them because of the great Lion

questions.prompt: Dorothy tells the woman the Lion “will be more afraid of you than you are of him.” Why is that a clever thing to say?
facilitatorNotes: It is true, and it makes the frightening Lion sound harmless, so the woman lets them in. Some children may say it is a little unkind to the Lion; ask how the Lion might feel hearing it.
evidence: he is a great coward, too; so that he will be more afraid of you than you are of him

readings.title: Oz, chapter X, part 2: what people say about Oz
readings.challenge: Separate what a character has seen from what he has only heard.
readings.focus: A farmer who has never seen Oz tells the travellers everything people say about him.
readings.context: Recap: Dorothy, her dog Toto, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion are walking to the Emerald City to ask the great Wizard Oz for help: Dorothy wants to go home to Kansas, the Scarecrow wants brains, the Tin Woodman a heart and the Lion courage. A farm woman in the green country has let them stay the night; her husband, who has hurt his leg, lies on the couch. Presence means being in the same room as someone; permitted means allowed.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, from the farmer’s question to bedtime at the farmhouse; opens “So they all entered the house, where there were, besides the woman, two children and a…”; closes “…stood up in a corner and kept quiet all night, although of course they could not sleep.”.

questions.prompt: What has the farmer seen of Oz, and what has he only heard?
facilitatorNotes: He has been to the Emerald City many times but has never seen Oz, and knows no one who has. All he says about Oz’s looks is what “some say.”
evidence: I have never been permitted to see the Great Oz
some say he looks like a bird

questions.prompt: What does the farmer say Oz keeps for each traveller?
facilitatorNotes: More brains than he needs, a large collection of hearts, and a great pot of courage covered with a golden plate. Ask whether he can really know this.
evidence: Oz has a large collection of hearts, of all sizes and shapes
Oz keeps a great pot of courage in his throne room

questions.prompt: Dorothy does not know where Kansas is. What does she say, and how does she feel?
facilitatorNotes: “I don’t know … but it is my home, and I’m sure it’s somewhere.” She is sad but still sure.
evidence: but it is my home, and I'm sure it's somewhere

questions.prompt: The farmer says Oz “can take on any form he wishes.” Why might a ruler nobody sees be talked about in so many ways?
facilitatorNotes: When no one sees him, people fill the gap with stories and guesses. Some children may simply believe Oz is magic; the next chapters let them test it.
evidence: Oz is a great Wizard, and can take on any form he wishes
who the real Oz is, when he is in his own form, no living person can tell

readings.title: Oz, chapter X, part 3: the green spectacles
readings.challenge: Ask why a rule exists, and who it helps.
readings.focus: At the gate of the Emerald City everyone must wear green spectacles that are locked on.
readings.context: Recap: Dorothy, her dog Toto, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion are walking to the Emerald City to ask the great Wizard Oz for help: Dorothy wants to go home to Kansas, the Scarecrow wants brains, the Tin Woodman a heart and the Lion courage. They spent the night at a farmhouse, where the farmer told them that no one ever sees the Great Oz. Studded means set all over; perplexity means puzzlement; an errand is a task; spectacles are glasses.

excerpt.locator: Chapter X, from the green glow in the sky to the end of the chapter; opens “The next morning, as soon as the sun was up, they started on their way, and soon saw a…”; closes “…gate, and they all followed him through the portal into the streets of the Emerald City.”.

questions.prompt: What do the travellers see before they reach the city, and what is the gate like?
facilitatorNotes: A green glow in the sky, then a high, thick green wall and a big gate studded with glittering emeralds.
evidence: a beautiful green glow in the sky
a big gate, all studded with emeralds

questions.prompt: How does the Guardian react when Dorothy asks to see Oz?
facilitatorNotes: He is so surprised that he sits down to think. No one has asked in many years, and he warns that Oz might destroy them if their errand is foolish.
evidence: The man was so surprised at this answer that he sat down to think it over.

questions.prompt: What reason does the Guardian give for the spectacles, and who holds the key?
facilitatorNotes: Without them the brightness of the city would blind them; they are locked on, and he has the only key.
evidence: the brightness and glory of the Emerald City would blind you
I have the only key that will unlock them

questions.prompt: Dorothy could not take the spectacles off even if she wished. What do you think of a rule like that?
facilitatorNotes: Some children will trust the reason given; others will wonder why glasses must be locked, and what the city looks like without them. Keep the question open for later chapters.
evidence: Dorothy could not take them off had she wished

readings.title: Oz, chapter XI, part 1: inside the Emerald City
readings.challenge: Picture a place from many small details, then notice what is missing.
readings.focus: The friends walk through a city where everything is green and wait to be called to Oz one at a time.
readings.context: Dorothy, her dog Toto, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion are walking to the Emerald City to ask the great Wizard Oz for help: Dorothy wants to go home to Kansas, the Scarecrow wants brains, the Tin Woodman a heart and the Lion courage. At the gate the Guardian locked green spectacles on all of them. Prosperous means well off; an audience is a meeting with a ruler; a counterpane is a bedspread; a wardrobe is a cupboard for clothes.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, “The Wonderful Emerald City of Oz,” from the green streets to the first night in the Palace; opens “Even with eyes protected by the green spectacles Dorothy and her friends were at first…”; closes “…upon the bed and rolled himself up like a cat and purred himself asleep in a minute.”.

questions.prompt: Name three green things in the city. Is there anything that is not green?
facilitatorNotes: Houses, pavement, windows, the sky, sunlight, candy, pop-corn, lemonade and pennies are all green. There are no horses or other animals at all.
evidence: Green candy and green pop-corn were offered for sale
There seemed to be no horses nor animals of any kind

questions.prompt: What does the soldier say about seeing Oz, and what are the rules for the visitors?
facilitatorNotes: He has never seen Oz; he speaks to him behind a screen. Oz will see each of them alone, only one each day.
evidence: I spoke to him as he sat behind his screen
each one of you must enter his presence alone, and he will admit but one each day

questions.prompt: How does each friend spend the night in a room meant for sleeping?
facilitatorNotes: The Scarecrow stands in the doorway watching a spider; the Tin Woodman moves his joints up and down; the Lion curls up on the bed like a cat and purrs himself to sleep.
evidence: he remained all night staring at a little spider
rolled himself up like a cat and purred himself asleep in a minute

questions.prompt: The narrator says the green girl’s politeness “was wasted on the Scarecrow.” Do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: A bed and a beautiful room are no use to someone who cannot rest or sleep. Some children may say the kindness still counts even if he cannot use it.
evidence: Of course this politeness was wasted on the Scarecrow

readings.title: Oz, chapter XI, part 2: Dorothy and the great Head
readings.challenge: Follow a bargain and decide whether it is fair.
readings.focus: Oz appears to Dorothy as a huge Head and will help her only if she kills the Wicked Witch of the West.
readings.context: Recap: Dorothy, her dog Toto, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion are walking to the Emerald City to ask the great Wizard Oz for help: Dorothy wants to go home to Kansas, the Scarecrow wants brains, the Tin Woodman a heart and the Lion courage. They are staying in Oz’s green palace, and he will see one of them each day. Dorothy goes first. In the first chapter her house fell on the Wicked Witch of the East, and the good Witch of the North kissed her forehead, leaving a mark. Meek means quiet and gentle; a charm is magic power.
readings.contentNote: Oz tells Dorothy to kill the Wicked Witch of the West; Dorothy weeps and says she has never killed anything willingly.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, from Dorothy’s walk to the Throne Room to her crying herself to sleep; opens “The next morning, after breakfast, the green maiden came to fetch Dorothy, and she…”; closes “…help her; so she went to her own room and lay down on the bed and cried herself to sleep.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Oz decide to see Dorothy after first being angry?
facilitatorNotes: The soldier tells him about her silver shoes and the mark on her forehead.
evidence: when I mentioned your silver shoes he was very much interested

questions.prompt: Oz calls himself “the Great and Terrible.” What does Dorothy call herself? Why is that a good answer?
facilitatorNotes: “Dorothy, the Small and Meek.” She answers in the same pattern but the opposite way, honest about who she is.
evidence: I am Oz, the Great and Terrible.
I am Dorothy, the Small and Meek.

questions.prompt: What does Oz ask her to do in return, and why does she say she cannot?
facilitatorNotes: Kill the Wicked Witch of the West. She has never killed anything on purpose; the Witch of the East “just happened.” She also asks how she could do what a great wizard cannot.
evidence: Kill the wicked Witch of the West
I never killed anything, willingly

questions.prompt: Oz says, “In this country everyone must pay for everything he gets.” Is his bargain fair to a little girl?
facilitatorNotes: Most children will say no: she is small, lost and only wants to go home. Some may say Oz has his reasons; notice that the eyes look at her “anxiously,” as if he needs her help.
evidence: In this country everyone must pay for everything he gets.
Help me and I will help you.

readings.title: Oz, chapter XI, part 3: a lovely lady and a terrible Beast
readings.challenge: Compare three visits that follow the same pattern but change one thing.
readings.focus: Oz appears to the Scarecrow as a lovely lady and to the Tin Woodman as a five-eyed Beast, and gives each the same answer.
readings.context: Recap: Dorothy, her dog Toto, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion are walking to the Emerald City to ask the great Wizard Oz for help: Dorothy wants to go home to Kansas, the Scarecrow wants brains, the Tin Woodman a heart and the Lion courage. Oz appeared to Dorothy as a great Head and said he would send her home only if she killed the Wicked Witch of the West. Dominions are the lands a ruler rules; to bestow is to give; gauze is thin cloth.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, from the Scarecrow’s call to the Throne Room to the Lion’s plan; opens “The next morning the soldier with the green whiskers came to the Scarecrow and said,”; closes “…to give us what we desire. So be of good cheer my friends for all will yet be well."”.

questions.prompt: How does Oz look to the Scarecrow, and how to the Tin Woodman?
facilitatorNotes: To the Scarecrow, a lovely lady with wings; to the Tin Woodman, a Beast as big as an elephant with five eyes, five arms and five legs.
evidence: a most lovely lady
a most terrible Beast

questions.prompt: What stays the same in every visit, whatever shape Oz takes?
facilitatorNotes: The same first words, “I am Oz, the Great and Terrible,” the question “Why should I do this?”, and the same price: kill the Wicked Witch.
evidence: I am Oz, the Great and Terrible
Help Dorothy to kill the Wicked Witch of the West

questions.prompt: Why does the Tin Woodman hope Oz will be the lovely lady and not the Head?
facilitatorNotes: He reasons that a head has no heart of its own and cannot feel for him, while ladies are said to be kind-hearted. He is thinking carefully, even though he says he has no heart.
evidence: a head has no heart of its own and therefore cannot feel for me

questions.prompt: The Lion plans to roar, pounce or roll the Head about. Do you think he will? Why?
facilitatorNotes: He sounds bold, but he is the Cowardly Lion, so children may predict he will be frightened. Others may say he is braver with his friends than he thinks. The next part tells.
evidence: If he is a beast when I go to see him, I shall roar my loudest
So be of good cheer my friends

readings.title: Oz, chapter XI, part 4: the Ball of Fire
readings.challenge: Notice how friends decide to do something none of them wants to do.
readings.focus: Oz appears to the Lion as a Ball of Fire, and the four friends decide to go together to find the Witch.
readings.context: Recap: Dorothy, her dog Toto, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion are walking to the Emerald City to ask the great Wizard Oz for help: Dorothy wants to go home to Kansas, the Scarecrow wants brains, the Tin Woodman a heart and the Lion courage. Oz has appeared to Dorothy as a Head, to the Scarecrow as a lovely lady and to the Tin Woodman as a terrible Beast, and has told each to kill the Wicked Witch of the West. The Lion boasted about what he would do. The Winkies live in the West; a grindstone sharpens tools.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XI, from the Lion’s visit to the end of the chapter; opens “The next morning the soldier with the green whiskers led the Lion to the great Throne…”; closes “…in the back yard of the palace, and the cackling of a hen that had laid a green egg.”.

questions.prompt: What happens to the Lion’s brave plan when he meets the Ball of Fire?
facilitatorNotes: The heat singes his whiskers, he creeps back to the door trembling, and at last he turns tail and runs. His boasts come to nothing.
evidence: he crept back tremblingly to a spot nearer the door
he turned tail and rushed from the room

questions.prompt: Each friend says what he will never have if they fail. Why does Baum line up their sentences one after another?
facilitatorNotes: It shows all four facing the same problem together, and builds to Dorothy, who will never see her family, and begins to cry.
evidence: And I shall never have brains
And I shall never see Aunt Em and Uncle Henry

questions.prompt: Each friend also says why he is not the right one to kill the Witch. What are their reasons?
facilitatorNotes: The Lion is too much of a coward, the Scarecrow says he is a fool, and the Tin Woodman hasn’t the heart to harm her. Each names exactly the thing he wishes for.
evidence: I'm too much of a coward to kill the Witch
I haven't the heart to harm even a Witch

questions.prompt: None of them wants to kill anybody, yet they all decide to go. Why?
facilitatorNotes: They each need what Oz promised, and they will not let Dorothy go alone. Some children may say they hope to find another way when they get there; the text leaves that open.
evidence: I am sure I do not want to kill anybody, even to see Aunt Em again
but if you go I certainly shall go with you

readings.title: Oz, chapter XII, part 1: the wolves
readings.challenge: Find the place where each friend becomes the one who can help.
readings.focus: The friends set out west, and the Witch sends a pack of wolves against them.
readings.context: Dorothy, her dog Toto, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion are walking to the Emerald City to ask the great Wizard Oz for help: Dorothy wants to go home to Kansas, the Scarecrow wants brains, the Tin Woodman a heart and the Lion courage. The great Oz has told each of them he will grant their wishes only when the Wicked Witch of the West is dead, so they are setting out to find her. The Winkies live in her country. Untilled means not farmed; a telescope makes far things look near.
readings.contentNote: The Tin Woodman kills forty wolves with his axe, one blow each; the deaths are told quickly and in a heap.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, “The Search for the Wicked Witch,” from the city gate to the morning after the wolves; opens “The soldier with the green whiskers led them through the streets of the Emerald City…”; closes “…saving them and sat down to breakfast, after which they started again upon their journey.”.

questions.prompt: How will the travellers find the Witch when there is no road?
facilitatorNotes: The Guardian says she will find them as soon as they are in the Winkie country; they should keep going west, where the sun sets.
evidence: when she knows you are in the Country of the Winkies she will find you

questions.prompt: What has happened to Dorothy’s green dress outside the city? What might that tell you?
facilitatorNotes: It is pure white, and so is Toto’s ribbon. Children may guess that the green came from the spectacles, not the cloth; it is a clue about the Emerald City.
evidence: she found it was no longer green, but pure white

questions.prompt: Why won’t the Witch make the travellers her slaves?
facilitatorNotes: She says none of them is fit to work: one is tin, one straw, one a girl and one a Lion.
evidence: None of them is fit to work

questions.prompt: The Tin Woodman says, “This is my fight.” Why is it his?
facilitatorNotes: He has an axe and a tin body that wolves’ teeth cannot hurt, and he is awake while the others sleep. Each danger in this chapter needs a different friend.
evidence: This is my fight
He seized his axe, which he had made very sharp

readings.title: Oz, chapter XII, part 2: crows, bees and Winkies
readings.challenge: Follow a pattern of three attacks and notice who answers each one.
readings.focus: The Witch sends crows, then bees, then her Winkie slaves, and each friend uses what he is to protect the others.
readings.context: Recap: Dorothy, her dog Toto, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion are walking to the Emerald City to ask the great Wizard Oz for help: Dorothy wants to go home to Kansas, the Scarecrow wants brains, the Tin Woodman a heart and the Lion courage. They are travelling west to find the Wicked Witch. She saw them with her one far-seeing eye and sent forty wolves, which the Tin Woodman killed with his axe. Forthwith means at once; to gnash teeth is to grind them in anger.
readings.contentNote: The Scarecrow kills forty crows by twisting their necks, the bees die when their stings break on the tin, and the Witch beats her Winkie slaves with a strap.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, from the Witch’s second whistle to her beating the Winkies; opens “Now this same morning the Wicked Witch came to the door of her castle and looked out with…”; closes “…was a powerful Witch, as well as a wicked one, and she soon made up her mind how to act.”.

questions.prompt: How do the crows behave when they see the Scarecrow, and what does the King Crow say?
facilitatorNotes: They are frightened, as crows always are of scarecrows, but the King Crow says he is only a stuffed man.
evidence: It is only a stuffed man.

questions.prompt: What is the Scarecrow’s plan against the bees, and why does it work?
facilitatorNotes: To cover Dorothy, Toto and the Lion with his straw, so the only one left to sting is the Tin Woodman, and the bees break their stings on his tin.
evidence: Take out my straw and scatter it over the little girl and the dog and the lion

questions.prompt: Why do the Winkies run away?
facilitatorNotes: They are not a brave people and only obey the Witch out of fear; when the Lion roars and springs at them, they run.
evidence: The Winkies were not a brave people, but they had to do as they were told

questions.prompt: The Scarecrow says he has no brains, and the Lion says he has no courage. What does this chapter show about them?
facilitatorNotes: The Scarecrow thinks of the clever straw plan, and the Lion scares off the Winkies. Children may notice that the friends already have some of what they want.
evidence: the Scarecrow had decided what to do
Then the Lion gave a great roar and sprang toward them

readings.title: Oz, chapter XII, part 3: the Winged Monkeys
readings.challenge: Notice a limit on magic and how it shapes what a character does.
readings.focus: The Witch uses the Golden Cap’s last call, and the Winged Monkeys scatter the friends but dare not harm Dorothy.
readings.context: Dorothy, her dog Toto, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion are walking to the Emerald City to ask the great Wizard Oz for help: Dorothy wants to go home to Kansas, the Scarecrow wants brains, the Tin Woodman a heart and the Lion courage. Hunting for the Wicked Witch of the West, they have beaten her wolves, crows and bees, and the Lion frightened off her Winkie slaves. A charm is magic; immense means huge; to harness is to strap an animal to a cart.
readings.contentNote: The Monkeys drop the Tin Woodman onto sharp rocks, pull the straw out of the Scarecrow and tie up the Lion; the friends seem destroyed.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, from the Golden Cap in the cupboard to the Monkeys’ flying away; opens “There was, in her cupboard, a Golden Cap, with a circle of diamonds and rubies running…”; closes “…much laughing and chattering and noise, flew into the air and were soon out of sight.”.

questions.prompt: What is the rule of the Golden Cap, and how many times has the Witch already used it?
facilitatorNotes: Its owner may call the Winged Monkeys three times only; she has used it twice, once to make the Winkies her slaves and once to drive Oz out of the West.
evidence: no person could command these strange creatures more than three times
Twice already the Wicked Witch had used the charm of the Cap.

questions.prompt: Why has the Witch saved the last call until now?
facilitatorNotes: Because it is the last; she uses it only when everything else, wolves, crows, bees and slaves, has failed.
evidence: she did not like to do so until all her other powers were exhausted

questions.prompt: What do the Monkeys do to the Tin Woodman, the Scarecrow and the Lion?
facilitatorNotes: They drop the Woodman on sharp rocks, pull out the Scarecrow’s straw and throw his clothes in a tree, and tie up the Lion and carry him to the Witch’s yard.
evidence: Here they dropped the poor Woodman
pulled all of the straw out of his clothes and head

questions.prompt: Why won’t the Monkeys harm Dorothy? What does their leader say about Good and Evil?
facilitatorNotes: They see the Good Witch’s kiss on her forehead; the leader says the Power of Good is greater than the Power of Evil. Children can talk about what that mark seems to mean.
evidence: she is protected by the Power of Good, and that is greater than the Power of Evil

readings.title: Oz, chapter XII, part 4: in the Witch’s castle
readings.challenge: Notice what one character knows that another does not.
readings.focus: The Witch makes Dorothy her servant and tries to starve the Lion, while Dorothy secretly feeds him.
readings.context: Recap: Dorothy and the Cowardly Lion are prisoners in the castle of the Wicked Witch of the West. Her Winged Monkeys dropped the Tin Woodman on rocks, emptied the Scarecrow of straw and tied up the Lion; they dared not harm Dorothy because of the Good Witch’s kiss on her forehead. A chariot is a two-wheeled cart.
readings.contentNote: The Witch threatens Dorothy, starves the Lion, and strikes Toto with her umbrella; Dorothy cries for hours.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, from the Witch’s first sight of Dorothy to Toto’s sorrow; opens “The Wicked Witch was both surprised and worried when she saw the mark on Dorothy's…”; closes “…was with him; but he knew the little girl was unhappy, and that made him unhappy too.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the Witch tremble when she first sees Dorothy, and why does she laugh instead?
facilitatorNotes: She sees the mark and the Silver Shoes and knows their power; then she sees in Dorothy’s eyes that the girl does not know how to use it.
evidence: the little girl did not know of the wonderful power the Silver Shoes gave her

questions.prompt: How does the Lion manage to say “No” every day without starving?
facilitatorNotes: Every night, while the Witch sleeps, Dorothy carries him food from the cupboard.
evidence: every night, while the woman was asleep Dorothy carried him food from the cupboard

questions.prompt: What does the narrator tell us that Dorothy does not know about the umbrella?
facilitatorNotes: The Witch threatens to beat her but dares not, because of the mark. Dorothy is afraid for nothing, and we know it.
evidence: she did not dare to strike Dorothy, because of the mark upon her forehead
The child did not know this

questions.prompt: How do Dorothy and the Lion help each other in the castle?
facilitatorNotes: She feeds him; he comforts her as she lies against his mane and they plan an escape. Toto, too, shows he is sorry when she cries. Ask which help matters more.
evidence: Dorothy would lie beside him and put her head on his soft, shaggy mane

readings.title: Oz, chapter XII, part 5: a bucket of water
readings.challenge: Find the clues that prepare for a surprising ending.
readings.focus: The Witch tricks Dorothy out of one Silver Shoe, and Dorothy’s angry bucket of water melts her.
readings.context: Recap: Dorothy works as the Wicked Witch’s servant while the Lion is shut in her yard. The Witch dares not hurt Dorothy, but she wants Dorothy’s magic Silver Shoes. Cunning means sly; invisible means unable to be seen.
readings.contentNote: The Witch melts away into a brown mass, and Dorothy sweeps it out of the door.

excerpt.locator: Chapter XII, from the Witch’s longing for the Silver Shoes to the end of the chapter; opens “Now the Wicked Witch had a great longing to have for her own the Silver Shoes which the…”; closes “…of the West had come to an end, and that they were no longer prisoners in a strange land.”.

questions.prompt: Why can’t the Witch steal the shoes at night or at bath time?
facilitatorNotes: She is afraid of the dark, and even more afraid of water.
evidence: her dread of water was greater than her fear of the dark

questions.prompt: What trick does the Witch use to get one shoe?
facilitatorNotes: She makes an iron bar invisible so Dorothy trips over it; one shoe comes off and the Witch snatches it.
evidence: she stumbled over the bar, not being able to see it

questions.prompt: Was Dorothy trying to destroy the Witch when she threw the water? How do you know?
facilitatorNotes: No. She was angry about the shoe; she is frightened and sorry when the Witch melts, and says she did not know water would do it.
evidence: I'm very sorry, indeed
Of course not," answered Dorothy; "how should I?

questions.prompt: Which clues earlier in the chapter point to water being the Witch’s weakness?
facilitatorNotes: She never touched water or let it touch her, and she feared it more than the dark. Some children may say they guessed; others that the ending surprised them. Both can point to the same sentence.
evidence: Indeed, the old Witch never touched water, nor ever let water touch her in any way.
